materials.text:
Now that you are holding onto a Node you have a few responsibilities:

First, you must read from the Node.Ready() channel and process the updates
it contains. These steps may be performed in parallel, except as noted in step
2.

1. Write HardState, Entries, and Snapshot to persistent storage if they are
not empty. Note that when writing an Entry with Index i, any
previously-persisted entries with Index >= i must be discarded.

2. Send all Messages to the nodes named in the To field. It is important that
no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk,
and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while
entries from the same batch are being persisted). To reduce the I/O latency, an
optimization can be applied to make leader write to disk in parallel with its
followers (as explained at section 10.2.1 in Raft thesis). If any Message has type
MsgSnap, call Node.ReportSnapshot() after it has been sent (these messages may be
large).

Note: Marshalling messages is not thread-safe; it is important that you
make sure that no new entries are persisted while marshalling.
The easiest way to achieve this is to serialize the messages directly inside
your main raft loop.

3. Apply Snapshot (if any) and CommittedEntries to the state machine.
If any committed Entry has Type EntryConfChange, call Node.ApplyConfChange()
to apply it to the node. The configuration change may be cancelled at this point
by setting the NodeID field to zero before calling ApplyConfChange
(but ApplyConfChange must be called one way or the other, and the decision to cancel
must be based solely on the state machine and not external information such as
the observed health of the node).

4. Call Node.Advance() to signal readiness for the next batch of updates.
This may be done at any time after step 1, although all updates must be processed
in the order they were returned by Ready.

Second, all persisted log entries must be made available via an
implementation of the Storage interface. The provided MemoryStorage
type can be used for this (if you repopulate its state upon a
restart), or you can supply your own disk-backed implementation.

Third, when you receive a message from another node, pass it to Node.Step:

	func recvRaftRPC(ctx context.Context, m raftpb.Message) {
		n.Step(ctx, m)
	}

Finally, you need to call Node.Tick() at regular intervals (probably
via a time.Ticker). Raft has two important timeouts: heartbeat and the
election timeout. However, internally to the raft package time is
represented by an abstract "tick".

The total state machine handling loop will look something like this:

	for {
	  select {
	  case <-s.Ticker:
	    n.Tick()
	  case rd := <-s.Node.Ready():
	    saveToStorage(rd.State, rd.Entries, rd.Snapshot)
	    send(rd.Messages)
	    if !raft.IsEmptySnap(rd.Snapshot) {
	      processSnapshot(rd.Snapshot)
	    }
	    for _, entry := range rd.CommittedEntries {
	      process(entry)
	      if entry.Type == raftpb.EntryConfChange {
	        var cc raftpb.ConfChange
	        cc.Unmarshal(entry.Data)
	        s.Node.ApplyConfChange(cc)
	      }
	    }
	    s.Node.Advance()
	  case <-s.done:
	    return
	  }
	}

To propose changes to the state machine from your node take your application
data, serialize it into a byte slice and call:

	n.Propose(ctx, data)

If the proposal is committed, data will appear in committed entries with type
raftpb.EntryNormal. There is no guarantee that a proposed command will be
committed; you may have to re-propose after a timeout.

# Usage with Asynchronous Storage Writes

The library can be configured with an alternate interface for local storage
writes that can provide better performance in the presence of high proposal
concurrency by minimizing interference between proposals. This feature is called
AsynchronousStorageWrites, and can be enabled using the flag on the Config
struct with the same name.

When Asynchronous Storage Writes is enabled, the responsibility of code using
the library is different from what was presented above. Users still read from
the Node.Ready() channel. However, they process the updates it contains in a
different manner. Users no longer consult the HardState, Entries, and Snapshot
fields (steps 1 and 3 above). They also no longer call Node.Advance() to
indicate that they have processed all entries in the Ready (step 4 above).
Instead, all local storage operations are also communicated through messages
present in the Ready.Message slice.

The local storage messages come in two flavors. The first flavor is log append
messages, which target a LocalAppendThread and carry Entries, HardState, and a
Snapshot. The second flavor is entry application messages, which target a
LocalApplyThread and carry CommittedEntries. Messages to the same target must be
reliably processed in order. Messages to different targets can be processed in
any order.

Each local storage message carries a slice of response messages that must
delivered after the corresponding storage write has been completed. These
responses may target the same node or may target other nodes.

After creating a Node, the user has a few responsibilities:

First, read from the Node.Ready() channel and process the updates it contains. These steps may be performed in parallel, except as noted in step 2.

1. Write Entries, HardState and Snapshot to persistent storage in order, i.e. Entries first, then HardState and Snapshot if they are not empty. If persistent storage supports atomic writes then all of them can be written together. Note that when writing an Entry with Index i, any previously-persisted entries with Index >= i must be discarded.

2. Send all Messages to the nodes named in the To field. It is important that no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk, and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while entries from the same batch are being persisted). To reduce the I/O latency, an optimization can be applied to make leader write to disk in parallel with its followers (as explained at section 10.2.1 in Raft thesis). If any Message has type MsgSnap, call Node.ReportSnapshot() after it has been sent (these messages may be large). Note: Marshalling messages is not thread-safe; it is important to make sure that no new entries are persisted while marshalling. The easiest way to achieve this is to serialise the messages directly inside the main raft loop.

3. Apply Snapshot (if any) and CommittedEntries to the state machine. If any committed Entry has Type EntryConfChange, call Node.ApplyConfChange() to apply it to the node. The configuration change may be cancelled at this point by setting the NodeID field to zero before calling ApplyConfChange (but ApplyConfChange must be called one way or the other, and the decision to cancel must be based solely on the state machine and not external information such as the observed health of the node).

4. Call Node.Advance() to signal readiness for the next batch of updates. This may be done at any time after step 1, although all updates must be processed in the order they were returned by Ready.

Second, all persisted log entries must be made available via an implementation of the Storage interface. The provided MemoryStorage type can be used for this (if repopulating its state upon a restart), or a custom disk-backed implementation can be supplied.

Third, after receiving a message from another node, pass it to Node.Step:

```go
	func recvRaftRPC(ctx context.Context, m raftpb.Message) {
		n.Step(ctx, m)
	}
```

Finally, call `Node.Tick()` at regular intervals (probably via a `time.Ticker`). Raft has two important timeouts: heartbeat and the election timeout. However, internally to the raft package time is represented by an abstract "tick".

feedback.answered: Source explanation for the selected prior-term inherited-tail context: let L be lastIndex during becomeLeader.reset and T the new leader term. reset sets self Match=L. becomeLeader then appends its empty entry at L+1 with term T; appendEntry leaves self Match unchanged and schedules its self MsgAppResp through the persistence queue. If quorum aggregation selects an index at or below L, that inherited entry has term below T by the selected context, so raftLog.maybeCommit rejects it. If aggregation selects an index above L, the initialized self Match does not support that index in either majority order statistic; the required majority must come from other progress or a subsequently processed self response. Therefore this initialized old frontier cannot provide the missing vote for committing a current-term index. This is a bounded inference from the actual reset, append and commit consumers, not execution Evidence. It does not prove uniqueness of leaders, legitimacy of arbitrary network/storage input, durable caller behavior, or safety of all configuration changes. A leader may legitimately commit with a sufficient remote quorum while its own write is pending; a requirement that every leader commit wait for local storage would be stronger than this explanation.

Node.ProposeConfChange promises dropping while a prior unapplied change may exist; Node.Advance generally permits overlapping application, while ApplyConfChange requires invocation whenever a committed change is observed. The source excerpts do not resolve whether configuration activation itself may be deferred across Advance. Entry and ownership: all mutations enter public RawNode methods under serialized driver ownership; private log/unstable access only reads observations. Five nodes start from the same documented storage-backed committed snapshot, then actual campaigns, votes, append rejection/retry and storage-request production create the three-term history. Initial snapshot/HardState assignment is an explicit caller prefix, not assigned critical replacement state. Caller duties: MemoryStorage is the declared no-crash persistence substitute. Each append request writes entries/HardState before responses; requests are FIFO. Node-2 local responses remain FIFO even while already-persisted responses to other recipients progress. Current replacement writes are held in a separate FIFO and all are completed later. Oracle and correlation: replacement serial 4 captures actual accepted work for op=replacement,node=2,entry_index=3, including Index/Term/Type/Data in a deterministic immutable JSON string. Admission serial 8 references serial 4 and independently records a stale MsgStorageAppendResp, pending write and conflicting stored entry. The identity fields do not include term or compared contents. No precondition tests the result log_entry or suppresses an unfavorable result. The result at serial 9 is produced after Step returns and directly queries raftLog.slice; it equals the captured expected entry, including payload. Admission and result are unique; retained monitor assessment reports matched prerequisites, one evaluated result, no missing observations and no parsing errors. Serial 10 shows the permitted current completion leaves the same logical entry while Storage term becomes 2 and unstable is empty; serial 11 reports empty queues and follower applied/commit 4. items.rationale:
Reviewed artifact fd9efd7d132b4ed39389868a253233bb version 1, its fixed plan and harness, claim C_PENDING_CONFIG_ADMISSION version 1, binding BIND_PENDING_CONFIG version 1, and actual execution 5f04338bd9e04060b57241324ec589da together. The runner completed all three subtests and recorded P_PENDING_CONFIG as violated. The relevant witness is op=second-config-deferred_early_advance, node=1, proposal_seq=2: first configuration index 3 term 2 was committed and saved; before the second proposal, internal Applied was 3 but caller activation was false and active voters were {1}. The actual result at index 4 was EntryConfChange, accepted_as_configuration=true, while first_pending_at_processing=true. This contradicts the fixed one-way admission predicate. The process passing is only driver completion, not a property hold.

Applicability is supported by the selected public Node contract. Node.ProposeConfChange requires dropping changes unless no prior unapplied change remains. The numbered Node usage instructions explicitly put configuration activation in step 3 and allow Advance at any time after persistence step 1. The selected caller completes persistence, eventually invokes ApplyConfChange for every delivered accepted configuration, and preserves application order across Ready batches. I interpret the separate whenever-observed duty as requiring handling each configuration, not an unstated deadline before Advance: imposing that deadline would negate the explicit permission for these same numbered steps. The driver neither rejects nor forgets the first change. The early case actually finishes by applying first then second and reaches voters {1,2,3}, Applied/commit 4. RawNode.Advance uses stricter applied-and-saved wording, but the driver invokes Node.Advance, whose public permission and usage steps define this scope. Existing tests using activation first demonstrate a conservative policy, not an exclusion of the documented overlap. This resolves the recorded immediate-duty counterinterpretation for this bounded Node contract; it does not claim all caller policies are legal or settle asynchronous APIs.

The actual prefix uses RestartNode over MemoryStorage snapshot/HardState index/term 1 and Config.Applied 1, followed by an actual election and two real ProposeConfChange calls. This valid supplied prefix avoids invented role or critical guard state. New peers do not run; their traffic is dropped. No target state is directly assigned, no inbound messages or ticks introduce a competing log producer, and no role change occurs in the interval. MemoryStorage replaces device persistence only in a no-crash scope. ProposeConfChange encodes MsgProp and sends it through Node.Step without waiting for processing, but the subsequent Status rendezvous is handled by the same loop after the proposal case runs r.Step. Thus the barrier, not nil proposal return, establishes processing before the caller captures pendingAtProcessing. ApplyConfChange returns only after the loop produces ConfState; the driver activation ledger is tied to that returned call, and the loop does not autonomously activate simple configuration entries. Public voter-set diagnostics agree with the ledger.

Monitor admission_alias explicitly selects proposal_admitted. first_committed is a separate predecessor with first_index linkage; op/node/proposal_seq uniquely correlates all records and is independent of compared values. Each policy has exactly one second proposal and one result, and its first post-prefix emitted entry is therefore uniquely associated with that proposal. The result is read from actual Ready.Entries Type; both configuration encodings count as acceptance. No desired outcome is used to filter admission or the result. first_pending_at_processing is captured before any later activation, independently of the result Type. In the no-Advance control the first configuration is applied after the processing barrier but before draining the second entry; the saved processing-time pending flag correctly remains true. Its result EntryNormal with empty data satisfies rejection. In the activation-first control pending is false, so the implication does not demand acceptance, rejection or commitment; the observed uncommitted configuration entry is permitted. Final cleanup and Stop do not depend on the property succeeding, and all three finished events are present with no timeout, panic or missing result.

The code path explains the observation: early Node.Advance processes a queued apply response, internal applied reaches pendingConfIndex, and stepLeader no longer rejects on the pending-index guard even though membership activation remains outstanding. That mechanism is source-grounded and consistent with the controls; the measured responsibility is the public admission promise, not a proof of the sole cause of broader consensus harm. The later commit of the second entry under voters {1} is a diagnostic endpoint, not an independently checked inconsistent-decision claim. No checker or requirement changes are needed for the executed version.
